paragraphs.source_en: The predominance of mouflon and antelope may also be an indicator of social identity. It is best evident if compared with the neighbouring artistic tradition, namely the Bubaline engravings discussed in the second chapter. These engravings are located on the borders of the Tassili Plateau and also in the Algerian Tadrart and in the Acacus, but they are not mixed with the Round Head paintings. Their main concentration is in the massif of Messak (next to the Acacus) which represents a similar special area for engravings as the Tassili Plateau did for the paintings. Bubaline engravings are probably at least partly contemporaneous with the Round Heads but they are so different in style and in themes that they must be attributed to a different culture.

units.source_en: Their main concentration is in the massif of Messak (next to the Acacus) which represents a similar special area for engravings as the Tassili Plateau did for the paintings.
Bubaline engravings are probably at least partly contemporaneous with the Round Heads but they are so different in style and in themes that they must be attributed to a different culture.

paragraphs.source_en: The most striking difference between the two artistic traditions is the almost total absence of mouflon and antelope in the Bubaline art. These engravings are dominated by representations of bovids and other large mammals such as elephants, which are extremely rare in the Round Head paintings. The exclusivity of different animal species in the two artistic complexes and their relative vicinity in space suggest that the respective selected animals represented the identity of these neighbouring cultures. Thus, Bubalus antiquus would represent not only the social identity of groups producing the Bubaline engravings but these animals carved in the rock would also serve as a visible mark of their cultural and (ritual) territory.
